claim: AWS RAM securely shares your resources across AWS accounts, within your organization or OUs, and with IAM roles and users for supported resource types, so a resource is created once and used by other accounts.
question: What is AWS RAM, and with whom can resources be shared?

values.display: securely share your resources across AWS accounts
create a resource once
with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and users

qualifiers.condition: IAM roles and users only for supported resource types

evidence.quote: AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) helps you securely share your resources across AWS accounts, within your organization or organizational units (OUs), and with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and users for supported resource types. If you have multiple AWS accounts, you can create a resource once and use AWS RAM to make that resource usable by those other accounts.

claim: With RAM you can share with all accounts in the organization or only with accounts in specified OUs, and you can also share with specific AWS accounts by account ID whether or not they are in an organization.
question: Can RAM share with an account that is not in the organization?

values.display: share resources with all the other accounts in the organization
share with specific AWS accounts by account ID
regardless of whether the account is part of an organization

qualifiers.condition: resource type must allow sharing outside the organization

evidence.quote: If your account is managed by AWS Organizations, you can share resources with all the other accounts in the organization or only those accounts contained by one or more specified organizational units (OUs). You can also share with specific AWS accounts by account ID, regardless of whether the account is part of an organization.

claim: RAM reduces operational overhead because a resource is created once and shared, so you do not provision duplicate resources in every account, and all users of a share are managed by a single set of policies and permissions.
question: What are the benefits of sharing a resource with RAM instead of duplicating it?

values.display: eliminates the need to provision duplicate resources
a single set of policies and permissions

evidence.quote: This eliminates the need to provision duplicate resources in every account, which reduces operational overhead.
Instead, all users of an AWS RAM resource share are managed by a single set of policies and permissions.

claim: Compared with sharing through a resource-based policy, RAM can share with an organization or OU without listing every account ID, and shared resources appear in the consumer's service console and APIs; resources shared by a resource-based policy are not visible this way and must be referenced by ARN.
question: When should you share with RAM instead of a resource-based policy?

values.display: without having to enumerate every one of the AWS account IDs
as if those resources were directly in the user's account
Resources shared by attaching a resource-based policy aren't visible this way

qualifiers.scope: AWS RAM compared with resource-based policies

evidence.quote: You can share with an organization or an organizational unit (OU) without having to enumerate every one of the AWS account IDs.
Users can see the resources shared with them directly in the originating AWS service console and API operations as if those resources were directly in the user's account.
Resources shared by attaching a resource-based policy aren't visible this way; instead, you have to discover and explicitly refer to the resource by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN).

claim: Sharing a resource grants principals in the consuming account access to it, and the policies and permissions that apply to roles and users in the consuming account also apply to the shared resource.
question: Do the consumer account's own IAM policies apply to a resource shared with RAM?

values.display: you are granting access for principals in the consuming account
also apply to the shared resource

evidence.quote: When you share a resource in the owning account with another AWS account, the consuming account, you are granting access for principals in the consuming account to the shared resource. Any policies and permissions that apply to roles and users in the consuming account also apply to the shared resource.

claim: To share within an organization you first enable sharing with AWS Organizations in RAM; then RAM sends no invitations and principals in the organization get access without exchanging invitations.
question: Are invitations needed when RAM shares inside an organization?

values.display: you must first use the AWS RAM console
AWS RAM doesn't send invitations to principals

evidence.quote: To share resources within an organization, you must first use the AWS RAM console or AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) to enable sharing with AWS Organizations. When you share resources in your organization, AWS RAM doesn't send invitations to principals. Principals in your organization gain access to shared resources without exchanging invitations.

claim: When RAM shares with an account outside the organization, it starts an invitation process and the recipient must accept the invitation before it can access the shared resources.
question: What is needed to share a resource with an account outside the organization?

values.display: AWS RAM initiates an invitation process
The recipient must accept the invitation

qualifiers.condition: resource type allows sharing outside the organization

evidence.quote: If you share resources with an account that isn't part of your organization, then AWS RAM initiates an invitation process. The recipient must accept the invitation before that principal can access the shared resources.

claim: Sharing with AWS Organizations must be enabled from the RAM console or CLI so that the RAM service-linked role is created; enabling trusted access from the Organizations console does not create the role, and then you cannot share within the organization.
question: Where must RAM sharing with AWS Organizations be enabled?

values.display: You must enable sharing with AWS Organizations
you can't share resources within your organization

evidence.quote: If you enable trusted access with AWS Organizations by using the AWS Organizations console or the enable-aws-service-access AWS CLI command, the AWSServiceRoleForResourceAccessManager service-linked role isn't created, and you can't share resources within your organization.
You must enable sharing with AWS Organizations by using the AWS RAM console or the enable-sharing-with-aws-organization AWS CLI command.

claim: By default, sharing within the organization restricts access to consumers in the same organization, so an account that leaves the organization loses access to the shared resources unless the share was created with RetainSharingOnAccountLeaveOrganization.
question: What happens to RAM shared resources when a consumer account leaves the organization?

values.display: that account loses access to resources in the resource share
RetainSharingOnAccountLeaveOrganization

evidence.quote: By default, when you enable sharing with AWS Organizations, resource sharing within your organization restricts access to consumers within the same organization. If a consumer account leaves the organization, that account loses access to resources in the resource share.

For account-to-account sharing within your organization, you can retain sharing access when accounts leave by setting RetainSharingOnAccountLeaveOrganization to True when you create a new resource share.

claim: You can add only your own organization and its OUs as principals of a resource share, not organizations or OUs from outside; outside principals can be added only as individual accounts or, for supported services, IAM roles and users.
question: Can a resource share include an OU or organization outside your own organization?

values.display: You can add only the organization your account is a member of
You can't add OUs or organizations from outside your own organization

evidence.quote: You can add only the organization your account is a member of, and OUs from that organization to your resource shares. You can't add OUs or organizations from outside your own organization to a resource share as principals. However, you can add individual AWS accounts or, for supported services, IAM roles and users from outside your organization as principals to a resource share.

claim: Sharing a resource with principals outside the owning account does not change the permissions or quotas that apply to the resource in the account that created it.
question: Does sharing a resource with RAM change its permissions or quotas in the owner account?

values.display: doesn't change the permissions or quotas
within the account that created it

evidence.quote: Sharing a resource with principals outside of the AWS account that owns the resource doesn't change the permissions or quotas that apply to the resource within the account that created it.

claim: Some resource types cannot be shared with any account outside the organization; an example is VPC subnets, and sharing them outside returns an error.
question: Which resource types can be shared only within the same organization?

values.display: Some resource types can’t be shared with any account
An example resource type with this restriction

evidence.quote: Some resource types can’t be shared with any account that isn't a member of that organization. An example resource type with this restriction is virtual private connections (VPCs) that are part of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).

note: d085; the AWS sentence names 'virtual private connections (VPCs)'; the shareable table names ec2:Subnet as organization-only (ram-share-subnets-only-within-organization)

claim: When trusted access between RAM and AWS Organizations is disabled, principals in the organization are removed from all resource shares and lose access to the shared resources.
question: What happens to organization principals when RAM trusted access is disabled?

values.display: principals within your organization are removed from all resource shares
lose access to those shared resources

evidence.quote: When you disable trusted access to AWS Organizations, principals within your organization are removed from all resource shares and lose access to those shared resources.

claim: Most resources shared with RAM are Regional: they exist in the Region where they were created, you must direct operations to that Region to use them, and a resource share is visible only in the Region where it was created.
question: Can a Regional resource shared with RAM be used from another Region?

values.display: Most resources that you can share with AWS RAM are Regional
you must direct your operations to that Region
visible in only the AWS Region in which it was created

evidence.quote: Most resources that you can share with AWS RAM are Regional. You create them in a specified AWS Region, and then they exist in that Region. To see or interact with those resources, you must direct your operations to that Region.
A resource share is visible in only the AWS Region in which it was created.

claim: AWS maps physical Availability Zones randomly to AZ names for each account, so us-east-1a in one account may be a different location in another; an AZ ID such as use1-az1 is the same physical location in every account, and a shared subnet is available in the consumer's AZ with the same AZ ID.
question: Why do AZ IDs matter when sharing subnets across accounts?

values.display: maps the physical Availability Zones randomly
the same physical location in every AWS account
whose AZ ID is also use1-az2

evidence.quote: AWS maps the physical Availability Zones randomly to the Availability Zone names for each AWS account.
For example, use1-az1 is an AZ ID for an Availability Zone in the us-east-1 Region and it represents the same physical location in every AWS account.

For example, if you share a subnet in the Availability Zone with the AZ ID use1-az2 with another account, this subnet is available to that account in the Availability Zone whose AZ ID is also use1-az2.

note: d089; the us-east-1a example sentence also on the page

claim: RAM has two types of managed permissions: AWS managed permissions, with one default permission for every supported resource type, and customer managed permissions that you author to grant only the actions you need (least privilege).
question: What are AWS managed and customer managed permissions in RAM?

values.display: AWS managed permissions and customer managed permissions
one default managed permission available for every resource type
that you author and maintain

evidence.quote: In AWS RAM, there are two types of managed permissions, AWS managed permissions and customer managed permissions.
AWS managed permission – There is one default managed permission available for every resource type that AWS RAM supports.

Customer managed permission – Customer managed permissions are managed permissions that you author and maintain by precisely specifying which actions can be performed under which conditions with resources shared using AWS RAM.

claim: After you create a resource share, RAM uses the managed permission to generate a resource-based policy that it attaches to each shared resource; the effect of a managed permission is always Allow.
question: How does RAM grant access to a shared resource behind the scenes?

values.display: generate a resource-based policy
the effect is always Allow

evidence.quote: After you create the resource share, AWS RAM uses the managed permission to generate a resource-based policy that is attached to each shared resource.
For a managed permission, the effect is always Allow.

claim: An SCP can prevent users from creating resource shares that allow sharing with principals outside the sharing user's organization, and another example SCP prevents users from accepting share invitations from external accounts.
question: How can SCPs restrict RAM sharing?

values.display: Prevent external sharing
principals that are outside of the sharing user's organization
Prevent users from accepting resource share invitations

evidence.quote: The following SCP prevents users from creating resource shares that allow sharing with principals that are outside of the sharing user's organization.
Example 1: Prevent external sharing
evidence.heading: Example Service Control Policies

evidence.quote: Example 2: Prevent users from accepting resource share invitations from external accounts outside your organization
evidence.heading: Example Service Control Policies

claim: In a shared VPC subnet, participants cannot work with route tables (they can only describe them) and cannot create, delete or describe NAT gateways.
question: Can a participant in a shared VPC subnet change route tables or create NAT gateways?

values.display: Participants cannot work with route tables
Participants cannot create, delete, or describe NAT gateways

qualifiers.scope: participants in a shared VPC subnet

evidence.quote: Participants cannot work with route tables (for example, create, delete, or associate route tables) in a shared VPC subnet. Participants can describe route tables in a shared VPC subnet.
Participants cannot create, delete, or describe NAT gateways in a shared VPC subnet.

claim: Only the VPC owner can attach a transit gateway to a shared VPC subnet; participants cannot.
question: Who can attach a transit gateway to a shared VPC subnet?

values.display: Only the VPC owner can attach a transit gateway
Participants can't

evidence.quote: Only the VPC owner can attach a transit gateway to a shared VPC subnet. Participants can't.

claim: Participants can create a limited set of VPC resources in a shared VPC, such as network interfaces and security groups, and those resources count against the participant account's VPC quotas, not the owner's.
question: Whose VPC quotas do a participant's resources in a shared VPC count against?

values.display: Participants can create a limited set of VPC resources
count against the VPC quotas in the participant account

evidence.quote: Participants can create a limited set of VPC resources in a shared VPC. For example, participants can create network interfaces and security groups, and enable VPC flow logs for the network interfaces that they own. The VPC resources that a participant creates count against the VPC quotas in the participant account, not the owner account.

claim: An invited account must accept the transit gateway resource share in RAM before it can use the transit gateway, and if Auto accept shared attachments was not enabled when the transit gateway was created, cross-account (shared) attachments must be accepted manually.
question: How are cross-account transit gateway attachments accepted?

values.display: You must accept the resource share
you must manually accept cross-account (shared) attachment
Auto accept shared attachments

qualifiers.condition: Auto accept shared attachments not enabled

evidence.quote: If you were added to a resource share, you receive an invitation to join the resource share. You must accept the resource share through the AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM) console before you can access the shared resources.

If you didn't enable the Auto accept shared attachments functionality when you created your transit gateway, you must manually accept cross-account (shared) attachment using either the Amazon VPC Console or the AWS CLI.
